In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and evaluation of methods for quantitative analysis of the BOLD effect in functional MRI (fMRI).
the development of new techniques and the improvement of the existing ones for the investigation of the human brain.
the investigation of the BOLD contrast in SE EPI at high field.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the intravascular component of the BOLD effect in SE EPI is composed of at least two fractions with different flow regimes and that the extravascular component is of the same order of magnitude as the intravascular one.
the intravascular contributions to the BOLD signal at TE = 80 ms and B0 = 3 T are dominated by a slow flow component, which is most probably related to the capillary bed, and a fast flow component.
the extravascular contribution is not negligible in SE fMRI, but that it is not dominant either.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the extravascular component of the blood oxygen level‐dependent ( BOLD ) effect is the main contributor to functional MRI ( fMRI ) at 3T.

at 3 T, the extravascular contribution is nearly as important as the intravascular one, and that the use of flow-compensated diffusion weighting in SE fMRI can improve the sensitivity to functional signal from the parenchyme.
at 3 T the BOLD effect at short TE can be attributed to both the intravascular and the extravascular space.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the BOLD contrast in SE fMRI is a combination of two components: a flow‐dependent component and a flow‐independent component.
there is a significant extravascular component in the SE‐EPI signal, and this component can be selectively suppressed by using a flow‐weighting scheme in combination with a 90° refocusing pulse.
the extravascular compartment contributes to the functional signal in spin‐echo fMR at high magnetic field strength.
